source.title: Dynamic compression and expansion in a classifying recurrent network
source.authors: M. Farrell; Stefano Recanatesi; Guillaume Lajoie; Eric T. Shea-Brown

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full preprint, including Results, Methods, Conclusions and Discussion, and the appendix.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different task and measure from the listed versions: it compares recurrent networks’ representation dimensionality with classification on held-out inputs or clusters. It reports its own results bearing on generalization, but does not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports generalization and representation-dimensionality results on synthetic cluster-classification tasks, plus an MNIST result referenced only as Fig. S4. It does not test random-label fitting, width past interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected models, optimizer comparisons, batch size effects on generalization, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. The MNIST result is cited in the text without a reported outcome here, so it is not a row.
record.test_reason: The study measures representation dimensionality and classification in recurrent networks, but none of V1–V8. Random labels are assigned to clusters, preserving within-cluster structure; this is not V1's random labeling of individual examples. The batch-size comparison measures compression, not held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors argue that chaos-driven expansion and learning-driven compression can produce compact, separable representations with good generalization. The proposed cost of lacking compression for localized inputs remains tentative, and the compression theory covers a simplified linear model.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains recurrent networks on synthetic delayed cluster-classification tasks, with a limited MNIST result referenced in the text; the listed versions concern other architectures, interventions and measurements. The task evaluates novel inputs and held-out clusters rather than fitting arbitrary labels and testing natural labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization and representation dimensionality vary with input ambient dimension, dynamical regime, and whether inputs are delivered to two neurons or distributed. The authors also state that more aggressive weight updates compress dimensionality faster.

fits_no_version.finding: Both dynamical regimes achieve perfect novel-sample accuracy with high-dimensional inputs; trained representations also permit perfect LR accuracy on clusters withheld from probe training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training these RNNs produces representations that support novel-sample classification and transfer across clusters for a linear probe.

fits_no_version.finding: Strongly chaotic networks have better LR generalization with distributed two-dimensional inputs; their generalization is less reliable with inputs restricted to two neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RNN representation generalization depends on dynamical regime and input geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation compression accompanies good generalization; localized inputs can yield expansion without clear compression and less reliable generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-dependent expansion and compression of RNN representations accompany differences in generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report compression only with minibatching for squared-error loss, but with both full batches and minibatches for cross-entropy with tanh.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size effects on representation compression depend on the loss and network nonlinearity.

record.problems: The classification tasks use synthetic Gaussian clusters with randomly assigned class labels and only two classes. The main RNN has 200 units, and the paper describes results as drawn from 30 network and input realizations. Some comparisons are described qualitatively rather than numerically in the text. The authors say broader tasks and input dimensions remain to be studied, and that their SGD compression theory has not been extended to the full nonlinear recurrent network trained over many samples.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. The MNIST result is mentioned only by reference to Fig. S4 without a result description in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Individual-example random-label fitting, natural-label comparison, and chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness rankings of generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, rather than judgments that the reported effects are absent. The record incorrectly says MNIST has no described outcome: the conclusion explicitly reports dimensionality compression on MNIST, although no accuracy result is supplied. This adds no evidence for a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep or test-error comparison around the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measure or comparison against norm- or margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: edge-of-chaos network
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective dimensionality of network responses through time.
rows.baseline: The trained network representation at t = 0 has ED approximately equal to that of the input.
rows.value: Dimensionality drops with increasing t and is highly compressed at teval = 10.
rows.locator: Results, “SGD trains networks to compress high-dimensional inputs”; Fig. 2e
rows.note: The paper reports dimensionality compression alongside perfect testing accuracy and held-out-cluster generalization; it does not report a quantified association across networks between ED and the train-test gap.
rows.check: Compression is supported. Effective representation dimensionality is not magnitude-aware weight sharpness or a train–test gap measure.

rows.subject: strongly chaotic network
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective dimensionality of network responses through time.
rows.baseline: The network first expands dimensionality until about t = 7, then reverses course to compress it up to t = 10.
rows.value: Expansion is much more dramatic for the strongly chaotic network; it achieves better generalization than the edge-of-chaos network.
rows.locator: Results, “Chaos drives dimensionality expansion, enabling SGD to find a balance between expansion and compression”; Fig. 3e
rows.note: The text links the expansion-then-compression pattern to the representation’s generalization properties but does not report a direct statistical relationship with a train-test gap.
rows.check: Separate the measures: Fig. 3e reports expansion until about t=7 followed by compression to t=10; better LR generalization belongs to Fig. 3g and R6. Neither tests a listed version.

rows.subject: strongly chaotic network
rows.operation_detail: Measured effective dimensionality of network responses through time.

conditions.value: two-dimensional input delivered to two randomly selected neurons

rows.baseline: The strongly chaotic network expands dimensionality without a clear compression phase.
rows.value: The ED remains small relative to the size of the network; the paper suggests the lack of compression may cost generalization, though generalization is relatively good.
rows.uncertainty: The paper states larger error bars for the generalization score in this condition.
rows.locator: Results, “Chaos drives dimensionality expansion, enabling SGD to find a balance between expansion and compression”; Fig. 4e and Fig. 4g
rows.note: The authors describe a possible generalization cost, not a measured correlation between ED and train-test gap.
rows.check: Separate dimensionality from generalization: expansion without clear compression is the ED result; larger error bars concern LR accuracy in R8. The proposed generalization cost is an interpretation.
